cases.abstract: Low-rank adaptation compresses weight updates, but its accuracy gap with full fine-tuning may also reflect how magnitude and direction are learned together. We introduce Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA), motivated by a VL-BART checkpoint analysis in which LoRA's magnitude and directional changes are positively correlated, unlike those of full fine-tuning. DoRA learns a separate magnitude vector and applies low-rank updates to normalized weight directions, allowing column lengths to change independently of the directional factors. Its adapted weights can be merged before inference. On eight commonsense benchmarks with pooled training data, LLaMA-7B reaches 78.4% average accuracy versus 74.7% for the reported LoRA baseline, training 0.84% rather than 0.83% of parameters. Halving DoRA's rank still yields 77.5% with a 0.43% trainable fraction. Image- and video-text evaluations also improve over LoRA, although the video-task aggregate remains below full fine-tuning. Detaching the normalization denominator reduces training memory relative to unmodified DoRA with small reported score changes. The results support separating magnitude learning from low-rank directional adaptation to improve the tested accuracy-parameter tradeoff.
cases.methods: DoRA represents each adapted weight column by a learned magnitude multiplying a normalized direction. Starting from the pretrained matrix W0, it sets the magnitudes to the original column norms and constructs directions from W0 + BA, where A and B are trainable low-rank factors and W0 remains frozen. Initializing B to zero preserves the pretrained weights at the start of fine-tuning. The normalization prevents directional-factor updates from directly setting column length, so the small magnitude vector supplies a separate degree of freedom without requiring a dense trainable matrix. Differentiating through this normalization projects directional gradients orthogonally to the current column direction. The experiments instead detach the denominator during backpropagation to reduce memory: the norm is recomputed during training, but its derivative is omitted. This approximation retains the forward parameterization while replacing the projected gradient with a scaled gradient.
cases.results: The rank sweep on LLaMA-7B illustrates a changed accuracy-parameter tradeoff, not a monotonic benefit from increasing rank. At rank 8, the reported average commonsense accuracy is 77.9% with DoRA and 40.7% with LoRA, although their trainable fractions differ only from 0.21% to 0.22%. DoRA at this rank also exceeds rank-32 LoRA's 74.7%, suggesting that the parameterization can matter more than rank in this setting. The advantage should not be read as immunity to capacity or optimization effects: DoRA falls to 61.9% at rank 4 and 72.1% at rank 64, compared with 78.4% at rank 32. Multimodal results likewise separate improvement over LoRA from recovery of full fine-tuning performance. On VL-BART video tasks, DoRA raises the reported aggregate score from 83.5 to 85.4 but remains below full fine-tuning's 87.5. Because these aggregates combine question-answering and captioning metrics, they describe benchmark-level gains rather than a uniform increase in accuracy.
cases.notes: Numerical comparisons use table entries rather than inconsistent narrative summaries; halved-rank LLaMA-13B DoRA scores 80.8 versus LoRA's 80.5, not the claimed one-point gain. The rank sweep is tied to its reported settings. Commonsense baselines for LLaMA-7B/13B and VL-BART baselines are taken from cited prior work; DoRA learning rates can differ. No statistical significance is inferred from tabulated means. Detaching the denominator omits the projection term in the exact directional gradient. The overhead ablation and main comparison report different LLaMA-7B scores and are not combined.

cases.abstract: We present GaLore, which reduces optimizer-state memory by compressing gradients rather than factorizing the weights being trained. Each update is optimized in a low-rank gradient subspace and then expanded to modify dense weights; refreshing the basis permits training to move beyond any one subspace. For specified gradient forms and conditions, the analysis bounds declining gradient stable rank and establishes conditional contraction of the projected gradient with fixed projections and an identity gradient regularizer. In C4 pretraining, a 1B model achieves validation perplexity 15.64 versus 15.56 for full-rank Adam and 19.21 for rank-matched LoRA, with equal learning-rate search budgets. At 7B, one distributed run reaches 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam after 19.7 billion tokens. Separate single-device profiling combines projection, 8-bit optimization, and per-layer updates to fit 7B training within 22.0 GB at small token batches, without offloading or checkpointing. The tested implementation reduces memory but also lowers throughput. GaLore therefore offers a measured memory-performance tradeoff for dense-weight pretraining and fine-tuning, rather than restricting adaptation to permanently factorized weights.
cases.methods: For a weight matrix with m <= n, GaLore obtains a rank-r left projection P from the leading left singular vectors of its gradient G. It forms R = P^T G and stores Adam's first and second moments in this smaller space, then applies a scaled, expanded update to the dense weight matrix. Thus the compressed objects are optimizer statistics, not a permanently low-rank weight factorization. Recomputing P at scheduled intervals lets accumulated updates span different subspaces while keeping state dimensions fixed. This refresh is consequential: the fixed-projection theorem concerns contraction within the selected subspace and does not establish convergence of the periodically changing Adam procedure. Refreshing too rarely can leave useful gradient directions outside that subspace; refreshing too often adds decomposition cost and can disrupt the usefulness of accumulated moments. The design therefore trades projection rank and refresh frequency against memory and optimization progress.
cases.results: At small per-GPU token batches, 8-bit GaLore reduces measured 7B training memory to 22.0 GB, 63.3% below BF16 Adam and 52.3% below 8-bit Adam, without checkpointing or offloading. This is a combined saving: projection reduces optimizer-state storage, while per-layer updates avoid retaining the full set of gradients. It should therefore not be attributed to low-rank projection alone. The separate 7B performance experiment used 64 A100 GPUs and a single trial, reaching perplexity 14.65 versus 14.61 after 19.7 billion tokens; it establishes close observed performance, not statistical equivalence or complete pretraining on a consumer GPU. Speed also limits the memory benefit. For a 1B model at a 256-token batch with per-layer updates, GaLore processes 1019.63 tokens per second, compared with 1205.31 for 8-bit Adam under the same update mode. These measurements favor GaLore when memory is the binding constraint, while exposing a throughput cost.
cases.notes: The fixed-projection result bounds the projected gradient under gradient-form, Lipschitz, bounded-weight, and contraction conditions with an identity regularizer. It is not a guarantee for Adam with basis refreshes or for global loss convergence. Table 2 uses parameter-plus-optimizer memory estimates; 22.0 GB refers to separate profiling, not the distributed performance run. Throughput comparisons pair the layerwise entries in Table 11 rather than combining its two update modes. Smaller-model token budgets differ between Table 2 and appendix Table 5, so those disputed counts are omitted.
